scope.start: 10b: R. Yosei bar Yehuda's shekel minimum for the redemption lamb, and the objection to it (opens mid-exchange)
scope.end: 11b: the redemption lamb that died before reaching the priest

sections.title: The Redemption Lamb: A Shekel Minimum, Any Value, or a Ragya?
sections.gist: Continuing the baraita on the repeated "you shall redeem": whether the lamb must be worth a shekel, how little suffices, and what one should give in practice.

bullets.text: The baraita read the repeated "you shall redeem" as teaching that the firstborn donkey (*peter chamor*) is redeemed at once and with a lamb of any value. Three questions follow: the source of R. Yosei bar Yehuda's shekel minimum, the ruling on it, and the practical advice R. Tarfon gave.

children.title: A Shekel Minimum? "All Your Valuations" vs. the Poor Man's Vow
children.gist: R. Yosei bar Yehuda takes his shekel from the verse on valuations; the Rabbis confine that verse to one who cannot afford his vow.

bullets.text: R. Yosei bar Yehuda: there is no redemption with less than a shekel.

Objection, whichever way you look at it: if the verse compares the *peter chamor* (firstborn donkey) to a firstborn son, the lamb should be worth five sela. If it doesn't, where does a shekel come from?

Answer: there is no comparison. The source is Rava's teaching on "And all your valuations shall be with the shekel of the Sanctuary" (Vayikra 27:25): no valuation you assess may be less than a shekel.

The comparison is imperfect: in valuations the money goes to the Temple, while the redemption lamb goes to a priest and carries no sanctity. R. Yosei bar Yehuda sees a shared structure of assessing value and transferring it.
The Rabbis: that verse is about affordability. One who vowed a person's valuation and lacks the funds pays at least a shekel, and the rule goes no further.
The context is the adjustment "according to what the vower can afford": the floor applies only when the fixed sum is reduced for a poor man.

children.title: Halakha Like the Rabbis: Even a Lean Lamb Worth a Ma'ah
children.gist: Rav Nachman rules that there is no minimum, Rav Yosef makes it concrete with a lean lamb worth a *ma'ah*, and the Gemara explains why that needed saying.

bullets.text: Rav Nachman: the halakha follows the Rabbis, so a lamb worth less than a shekel works.
How little? Rav Yosef: even a lean lamb (*patruza*) worth a *ma'ah*. Rava: the Mishnah (9a) already allows "a big or a small lamb".
Isn't this obvious, since the baraita allows any amount? Rav Yosef's ruling rules out two errors: that so little value is too little, and that a lean lamb is unfit because of its physical state.
So neither value nor physical quality sets a floor. The animals that are unfit for redemption are listed in the next Mishnah (12a).

children.title: Sela, Shekel or Ragya: Advice When Asked vs. Acting on One's Own
children.gist: R. Tarfon grades the lamb by the owner's generosity, Rava fixes the norm at a *ragya*, and the Gemara reconciles this with "any value".

bullets.text: R. Yehuda Nesia sent his *peter chamor* to R. Tarfon and asked how much he must give a priest.
R. Tarfon: the Sages said that a generous person gives a lamb worth a sela, a miserly person one worth a shekel, and an intermediate person one worth a *ragya*.
Rava: the halakha is a *ragya*, worth three dinars. It is named for being "close" (*ragil*) to both the sela (four dinars) and the shekel (two dinars).
Contradiction with Rav Nachman's "any value". Answer: one who comes to consult is told three dinars. One who acts on his own has fulfilled his obligation even with a lamb worth a *ma'ah*.
A parallel with *terumah*: a single grain exempts the whole pile, but one who asks the Sages is told a fortieth to a sixtieth, depending on his generosity.
Sending the donkey along may suggest that the answer could depend on the donkey's own value. R. Tarfon was himself a priest, which may be why he gave a range rather than a single figure.

sections.title: Redeeming by Value: R. Shimon Only, or R. Yehuda Too via Hekdesh?
sections.gist: Reish Lakish lets the owner redeem with the donkey's value. The Gemara first ties this to R. Shimon, then Ravina grounds it even for R. Yehuda in the laws of *hekdesh*.

children.title: Reish Lakish's Ruling: R. Shimon's Alone? Ravina's Objection
children.gist: Since R. Yehuda insists on a lamb, the ruling seems to follow R. Shimon; Ravina objects that the halakha and the unattributed Mishnah follow R. Yehuda.

bullets.text: R. Yitzchak citing Reish Lakish: one who has a *peter chamor* but no lamb redeems it with money equal to the donkey's value and gives that to a priest.
Whose view is this? R. Yehuda holds that the Torah insists on a lamb (9a), so it must be R. Shimon's. Rav Acha taught it that way.
R. Yehuda's insistence on a lamb belongs with his view that redemption is a real ritual, and that the donkey is *asur be'hana'ah* (forbidden in benefit) until it is performed.
Ravina objects. Wherever R. Yehuda and R. Shimon disagree, the halakha follows R. Yehuda.
Moreover, the unattributed Mishnah (9a), in which a doubtful donkey is redeemed with a lamb that the owner keeps, follows R. Yehuda (9b). Can Reish Lakish rule like R. Shimon?

children.title: Not Stricter Than Hekdesh: The Lamb Is a Leniency
children.gist: Ravina: even R. Yehuda agrees, since *hekdesh* (consecrated property) is redeemed with anything of equal value, and the lamb was given to make things easier.

bullets.text: Ravina: the ruling holds even for R. Yehuda. A *peter chamor* should not be stricter than *hekdesh*, which is redeemed with any movable property worth its value.
The Torah named a lamb not to be strict with the owner but to be lenient, so that he need not pay the donkey's full value. A lamb is worth less than a donkey.
Rav Nachman son of Rav Yosef redeemed a *peter chamor* with boiled vegetables worth its value.
Either route works on both views: a lamb of any value, or anything else worth the full value of the donkey.
Should the owner then add a fifth, as one does when redeeming *hekdesh*? The comparison is applied only as far as the Gemara applies it: value suffices, and a third party may redeem.

sections.title: Redeeming Another's Donkey: Does the Redeemer or the Owner Keep It?
sections.gist: Rav Huna validates a stranger's redemption. The Gemara asks who then owns the donkey, and Rav Nachman proves from the double payment that it stays the owner's.

children.title: Like Hekdesh, or the Owner Owns the Difference?
children.gist: For R. Shimon the donkey is plainly the owner's. For R. Yehuda the question is whether it resembles *hekdesh*, which goes to whoever pays, or whether the owner holds a stake in it.

bullets.text: Rav Sheizevi citing Rav Huna: if one redeems another's *peter chamor*, the donkey is redeemed.
Question: does the redeemed donkey belong to the redeemer or to the owner?
On R. Shimon's view there is nothing to ask. The owner may use the donkey for labor or rent it out even before redemption, so it is his, and giving a lamb to the priest changes nothing.
On R. Yehuda's view it is *asur be'hana'ah* before redemption, so it seems not to be the owner's until it is redeemed.

One side: it is like *hekdesh*, where "he will give the money and it will be assured to him" (Vayikra 27:19), so whoever pays acquires it. The other side: the owner may redeem with a cheaper lamb, so he owns the difference, which is unlike *hekdesh*.
If the redeemer kept it, people would roam the markets redeeming valuable donkeys with cheap lambs. And the redeemer here acts on his own, not as the owner's agent.

chart.caption: On R. Yehuda's view: two ways to classify the *peter chamor* before redemption
columns: Who keeps it when another redeems
rows: "He will give the money and it will be assured to him"
He may redeem with a lamb worth less than the donkey

children.title: Rav Nachman's Proof: The Thief Pays Double, So It Is Not Hekdesh
children.gist: A baraita obliges the thief of an unredeemed *peter chamor* to pay double. That must follow R. Yehuda, and double payment is never owed for Temple property.

bullets.text: Baraita: one who steals another's unredeemed *peter chamor* pays the double payment to the owner. The owner has no rights in it now, but he has rights afterward, once it is redeemed.
This must be R. Yehuda's view, since for R. Shimon the owner does have rights in it now.
If it were like *hekdesh*, there would be no double payment: "and it be stolen from the man's house" (Shemot 22:6) excludes theft from the Temple treasury.
So the *peter chamor* is not *hekdesh*. If another redeems it, it still belongs to the owner, and this is a clear proof.
The comparison to *hekdesh* has limits. It allows redemption by value and by a third party, but it does not strip the owner of title, because being *asur be'hana'ah* is not sanctity.

sections.title: Separate but Keep: When the Priest Has No Claim
sections.gist: Four cases where one must redeem or separate yet may keep the gift: doubtful donkeys, gifts inherited through a priest grandfather, produce bought from a gentile, and produce left with a gentile.

bullets.text: In each case the act that lifts the forbidden status (redemption or separation) is still required. Only the duty to hand the gift over falls away, because of the doubt or because of the path by which the owner acquired it.

rows: Yes: ten lambs, which are then tithed
A priest cannot prove his claim to any of them

As if the grandfather had separated them and bequeathed them
"I came through a man you cannot litigate with"

children.title: Doubtful Donkeys: The Lamb Enters the Pen for Ma'aser Behemah
children.gist: The Mishnah's lamb that is "tithed with non-sacred animals" cannot be the priest's. It belongs to an Israelite who redeems ten doubtful donkeys and keeps the lambs.

bullets.text: The Mishnah (9a): two donkeys, one that had given birth before and one that had not, bear a male and a female. One lamb is designated because of the doubt, and it is tithed with the non-sacred animals. A baraita asks: in what case does it enter the pen for the animal tithe (*ma'aser behemah*)?
Not once it reaches a priest. An animal bought or received as a gift is exempt from the *ma'aser behemah* (animal tithe) (mishna 55b), and the lamb is a gift to the priest.
Rather, an Israelite with ten doubtful firstborn donkeys designates ten lambs, tithes them, and they are his.
This supports Rav Nachman citing Rabba bar Avuh, who rules the same case the same way: a priest cannot prove that he is entitled to any of the ten.
The lambs are his by the rules of money, so using them in a conditional redemption does not take them out of his flock for tithing.

children.title: Inherited Through a Priest Grandfather: Donkeys and Produce
children.gist: Rav Nachman rules that an Israelite who inherits firstborn donkeys or *tevel* (untithed produce) through a priest keeps what he separates, and the Gemara explains why both cases are needed.

children.title: Ten Certain Donkeys and *miruach*: As If the Grandfather Separated
children.gist: The grandson must still redeem or separate, but keeps the lambs and gifts as though his priest grandfather had separated them and left them to him.

bullets.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabba bar Avuh: an Israelite has ten certain firstborn donkeys, inherited from his mother's father, a priest, who had inherited them from his own mother's father, an Israelite.
The donkeys needed redemption from the start. The priest should have redeemed them with lambs, but he could keep the lambs himself.
So the grandson designates ten lambs, tithes them, and they are his, as if his grandfather had designated them and bequeathed them to him.
Likewise with *miruach* (smoothed piles) of *tevel* that came down the same chain: he separates *terumah* and tithes and they are his, as if his grandfather had tithed, acquired and bequeathed them.
The priest grandfather could keep even the first tithe, which may be given to a priest.

children.title: Why Both Cases: Lambs Already Stand Apart vs. Produce Tithed From Itself
children.gist: Each case has a feature that might have made it unique: the priest's lambs already stand separate, while produce contains its own gifts.

bullets.text: From the donkeys alone, one might say the lambs "stand separated": the priest could simply declare that his own lambs redeem the donkeys.
Produce, though, needs its *terumah* separated and declared before a priest acquires it. So perhaps priestly gifts not yet separated are treated as not separated, even in a priest's hands.
From the produce alone, one might say it works only because the produce can be tithed from itself, the gift lying within the pile. A donkey needs a lamb brought from elsewhere.
So both rulings are needed.

children.title: Bought From a Gentile: Tithe the *miruach*, but Keep the Tithes
children.gist: R. Chanina: a Jew who buys *miruach* from a gentile must tithe them, because the land stays obligated, but he keeps the gifts, since the priest could never have claimed them from the gentile.

bullets.text: R. Shmuel bar Natan citing R. Chanina: one who buys *tevel* in *miruach* from a gentile tithes it, but the gifts are his. He need not give the *terumah* to a priest or the tithes to a Levite.

Who smoothed the piles? Not the gentile: "your grain" (Devarim 12:17, 18:4) limits *terumah* and tithes to grain whose processing a Jew completed. So a Jew smoothed them while they were still the gentile's.
He must tithe, because a gentile's ownership of land in Eretz Yisrael does not cancel its sanctity and free its produce from tithes.
But the gifts are his. He says to the priest: "I came to own this through a man with whom you cannot litigate."
The argument is striking: a claim that could never be enforced against the gentile is treated as extinguished for the Jewish buyer too.

children.title: Deposited With a Gentile: Demai, and Terumah Gedolah vs. Terumat Ma'aser
children.gist: Produce returned by a gentile seems to require giving *terumah* to a priest, against R. Chanina. Rav Dimi splits the portions, and Abaye supplies a verse for *terumat ma'aser*.

bullets.text: Mishnah (Demai 3:4): produce deposited with a Samaritan or an *am ha'aretz* keeps its status for tithes and Sabbatical-year produce. They are not suspected of exchanging it.
Deposited with a gentile, it is treated as the gentile's own produce, since he presumably exchanged it. R. Shimon: it is *demai*, since it is uncertain whether he exchanged it.

R. Elazar: all agree that one must separate *terumah* and tithes. They disagree about giving. The first tanna holds that the gentile certainly exchanged it, so the *terumah* goes to a priest. R. Shimon holds it is *demai*, so the priest must bring proof.
Rav Dimi taught this. Abaye objected: then if the exchange were certain, all would agree that one gives to a priest. Yet R. Chanina says that one who buys *miruach* from a gentile keeps the gifts.
Rav Dimi: perhaps the Mishnah means *terumah gedolah*, while R. Chanina means *terumat ma'aser*, the *terumah* separated from the tithe.

Abaye recalls R. Yehoshua ben Levi: "When you take the tithe from the children of Israel" (Bamidbar 18:26). Produce bought from Israelites has its *terumat ma'aser* separated and given to a priest. From produce bought from a gentile, one does not separate *terumat ma'aser* and give it to a priest.
Tosafot: the plain sense of the verse is a gentile who gave his tithe to a Levite, who then need not separate *terumat ma'aser* from it.
Whether one must separate and to whom the portion goes are separate questions. The path by which the produce was acquired affects only the giving.

chart.caption: Demai 3:4: produce returned by a gentile

sections.title: The Redemption Lamb That Died: Already in the Priest's Possession
sections.gist: On the Mishnah's clause "if it dies, one may derive benefit from it": even if the lamb dies in the owner's house, the priest benefits, because it became his once it was separated.

bullets.text: The Mishnah (9a) says of the redemption lamb: "if it dies, one may derive benefit from it". Where did it die? In the priest's house, the ruling is obvious, since it is his. In the owner's house before it was handed over, with the priest benefiting? That seems obvious too.
Answer: one might have thought that the priest acquires only once the lamb reaches him. The Mishnah teaches that from the moment the Israelite separated it, it stands in the priest's possession.
So a lamb that was alive when it was designated discharges the redemption. The owner need not redeem again, and he hands over the carcass.

Tosafot: the blessing is recited at the redemption, when the lamb is designated, not when it is handed over. Compare the end of Hullin, where the priestly gifts (*matnot kehunah*) belong to the priesthood before any priest receives them.

illustration.caption: The Gemara's reading of the Mishnah's clause: once the owner separates the lamb it stands in the priest's possession, so even if it dies in the owner's house the priest may derive benefit from it (Bekhorot 11b).

key_terms.definition: The firstborn male of a donkey, which its Israelite owner must redeem with a lamb given to a priest; if he does not redeem it, its neck is broken.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The daf sets how little the redemption lamb may be worth, allows redemption by the donkey's value or by a stranger, and asks who keeps the donkey afterward.

key_terms.sense: a prohibition on deriving any benefit
key_terms.definition: A prohibition not only on eating an item but on any use or profit from it, such as selling it, renting it out or working with it.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Yehuda holds the unredeemed firstborn donkey forbidden in benefit and R. Shimon permits it, and this decides both the attribution of Reish Lakish's ruling and the question of who owns the donkey.

key_terms.definition: Property dedicated to the Temple treasury. It may not be used for private benefit and can be redeemed for its value, after which it returns to ordinary use.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The firstborn donkey is "not stricter than consecrated property", so it may be redeemed by its value, but the double payment for its theft shows that it is not *hekdesh* in ownership.

key_terms.definition: The tithe of cattle and sheep: each year's newborn animals pass through a pen and every tenth is designated holy. Animals bought or received as gifts are exempt.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Mishnah's redemption lamb that enters the pen for tithing must be one an Israelite kept for doubtful donkeys, since a priest's lamb is a gift and exempt.

key_terms.sense: produce from which the gifts have not been separated
key_terms.definition: Produce whose obligation of terumah and tithes has taken effect but which has not yet had them separated. It is forbidden to eat until they are separated.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Untithed produce inherited through a priest or bought from a gentile must still have its gifts separated, even when the owner may keep them.

key_terms.sense: smoothing the grain pile, completing its processing
key_terms.definition: Smoothing the heap of threshed grain, the final stage of processing, at which the obligation to separate terumah and tithes takes effect.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Chanina's case requires that a Jew, not the gentile, smoothed the piles, since grain whose processing a gentile completed is not "your grain".

key_terms.sense: the terumah separated from the Levite's tithe
key_terms.definition: The tenth that a Levite separates from the tithe he receives and gives to a priest; it has the sanctity of terumah.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Dimi limits R. Chanina's ruling to *terumat ma'aser*, and R. Yehoshua ben Levi derives from "from the children of Israel" that produce bought from a gentile is exempt from giving it.

key_terms.definition: Produce acquired from someone not trusted to have tithed it. By rabbinic law it must be tithed out of doubt, but the gifts need not be given to a priest without proof.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Shimon rules that produce returned by a gentile depository is *demai*, so it is separated but the priest must bring proof to receive it.

judgment_calls: The four 'separate but keep' cases (doubtful donkeys, the priest grandfather, produce bought from a gentile, the gentile deposit) are grouped under one top-level section because they share one question: when must one separate but need not give? Each could instead be its own top-level section; the grouping keeps the thread visible, and the shiur points to the same parallel.

The doubtful-donkey baraita (11a.17–19) returns to the Mishnah on 9a, which is outside this outline, so it has no returns_to link. It was placed in the 'separate but keep' group rather than on its own.
Rav Nachman's two inheritance rulings are kept in one child (s14), with the 'why both are needed' passage as a sibling (s15), rather than splitting the donkeys and the produce into separate sections.
The dead-lamb passage (11b.10–11) is Gemara on a clause of the 9a Mishnah, not a new Mishnah, so its heading does not start with 'Mishnah:'.
The inheritance illustration runs the generations left to right in time order, whereas the text names the grandson first; a genealogy reads more naturally as a timeline.
coverage_notes: The shiur's opening (the betrothal-with-a-peter-chamor context on 10b) is outside this scope; 10b.31–11a.1 is outlined here from the shiur and the text.
The essay attributes the valuation-verse derivation to 'Rabba'; the text has Rava. Followed the text.

The essay calls the sages 'Rav Tarfon' and 'Rav Yehuda Nesia' and mentions 'Rabbi Yannai Mi-Si'ah'; the text has R. Tarfon and R. Yehuda Nesia, and no R. Yannai. Followed the text and omitted R. Yannai.
The essay names the middle coin 'bargaya/birgiya'; the text has ragya. Followed the text.
The essay says Rav Nachman b'Rav Yitzchak redeemed with herbs; the text says Rav Nachman son of Rav Yosef, with boiled vegetables. Followed the text.

The essay has Rav Huna's statement say the lamb belongs to the priest; the text says only that the donkey is redeemed. The bullets follow the text; the illustration shows the lamb going to the priest as the standard law of the redemption lamb.

The essay does not name Rav Dimi, Abaye or R. Yehoshua ben Levi in the gentile-deposit exchange and calls Rav Dimi's answer 'the Gemara's'; the text sets it as Abaye's objection, Rav Dimi's 'perhaps', and Abaye's citation of R. Yehoshua ben Levi. Followed the text.

The essay says the exception covers all of terumah gedolah and ma'aser except terumat ma'aser; the text contrasts only terumah gedolah (the Mishnah) with terumat ma'aser (R. Chanina). Followed the text.
The essay calls the dead-lamb passage the perek's final Mishnah; the text is the Gemara explaining a clause of the 9a Mishnah. Followed the text.
Text spelling: Rav Sheizevi (essay: Rav Shizbi); Rabba bar Avuh (essay: Rabbah bar Avuha). Followed the text.
